description: A small rectangular platform, some 25m by 4m, cut 1.5m back into the slope on the south side of Garden Wood. A short Terrace extends for 26m eastwards from the platform. On the western side, the platform is cut by a small quarry (NTSMR 01596). The purpose of this feature is unclear but it is possible that a small building may have stood here, perhaps an ornamental structure connected with Sutton Hoo House. title: Pillbox, Sutton Hoo
description:
Pillbox 1, situated on the crest of the hill to command an extensive view of the Deben. Built early in WWII, it is of the hexagonal type 22, the standard rifle and light machine gun (LMG) pillbox for 6 men, constructed of shuttered concrete with a smooth finish and traces of camouflage paint. There are six embrasures, five of identical pattern placed centrally to each face suitable for rifle or LMG, and a sixth for rifle only, adjacent to the entrance. The five embrasures have splayed and stepped side walls, inside and out (to prevent ricochets) and an internal splay to their upper surfaces. The entrance is protected by an L shaped blast wall, butt adjoined to the main structure and further secured by a metal tie rod above the entrance. The blast wall is pierced by a rifle embrasure, which aligns with the one adjacent to the entrance, enabling a field of view to the river.
The interior is half whitewashed and has a central brick roof support. Beneath the five embrasures are remains of hinged shelves for ammunition and support for the weapon. Each embrasure is 0.25m wide and 0.22m deep.
Several small holes in the vicinity of the pill box may have been slit trenches [SNA63094]

title: Evaluation at Sutton Hoo Farm, Sutton, Suffolk
description: The evaluation fieldwork comprised the excavation of three trenches ; 3no 15m x 1.8m trenches. The trenches were located to test a representative 5% sample of the area, targeting the areas of greatest impact from construction activity and landscaping and to identify any below-ground heritage assets. With the agreement of SCCAS, one of the four trenches agreed in the WSI (Trench 4) could not be excavated as it was situated in an active car park, Trench 1 was also reorientated to avoid the car park. In June 2024, Cotswold Archaeology carried out an archaeological evaluation at Sutton Hoo Farm, Sutton, Suffolk. A total of three trenches were excavated. The site was largely devoid of archaeological resource, with the exception of a single undated ditch.

title: Sutton Hoo, Changing Places Project, Sutton, Suffolk
description: The archaeological monitoring and recording comprised the observation by a competent archaeologist of all intrusive groundworks associated with the proposed development. These works comprised the machine excavation of the extension's foundation trench and an associated service trench. Archaeological features/deposits were investigated, planned and recorded. A metal-detecting survey of the resultant spoil from the monitored excavations was carried out but no pre-modern artefacts were recovered. Deposits were assessed for their palaeoenvironmental potential but no deposits were identified that required sampling. In January 2025, Cotswold Archaeology carried out a programme of archaeological monitoring and recording at Sutton Hoo, Sutton, Suffolk, during groundworks associated with the construction of an extension to the Visitor Welcome Centre, being undertaken as part of the Changing Places Project. Monitoring of a footing trench for the extension indicated the area had been truncated, probably by previous construction work, and no pre-modern features were identified. A probable ditch was noted running across the base of a service trench, the excavation of which was also monitored as part of this project. This ditch is coincidental in alignment to a feature interpreted as part of a Late Bronze Age/Iron Age field system recorded during an archaeological excavation undertaken in 2000. No artefacts were recovered during the archaeological monitoring. Metal detecting of the resultant spoil also failed to identify any pre-modern artefacts.

title: Hollow way, Sutton Hoo
description: An east-west hollow way descending the slope from a point at the northern end of the barrow cemetery to join the present track from Little Sutton Hoo.. It is 11.5m across and up to 1m deep, the northern side smooth and gradual while the southern side is much steeper and broken. There are traces of a broad flattened bank 0.9m wide, adjoining the eastern end along the south side. This hollow way and its continuation as the existing track to Little Sutton Hoo is part of an old route from the Deben ferry across the heath, which appears on John Norden's map of 1600-1 and on the 1629 map. It was also the link between the settlement at Little Sutton Hoo on the low ground and its sheepwalk on the plateau [SNA63094]

description: A very spread bank, 5.6m wide and 0.4m high, along the south eastern edge of a shelter belt and cut by the approach track to Sutton Hoo. It is on the same alignment as a prehistoric field system, now ploughed out in fields immediately to the south and is conceivably of that date [SNA63094]

title: GARDEN FIELD, SUTTON HOO
description: Site/SMR Code: BML037. In March 2016 Suffolk Archaeology Community Interest Company undertook a detailed fluxgate gradiometer and magnetic susceptibility meter survey on land currently set aside for sheep pasture at Garden Field, Sutton Hoo, Suffolk. The detailed fluxgate gradiometer survey was successful in recording a range of geophysical anomalies that complement the preceding non-intrusive surveys. Positive linear trends indicative of former settlement ditches or field boundaries from at least three separate phases, thermoremanent responses indicative of a kiln type anomaly, a plethora of discrete pit type anomalies, two areas of magnetic disturbance and sparse isolated dipolar responses of potential archaeological derivation, one broad geological anomaly, a dipolar linear trend delineating a modern service run and negative linear trends of agricultural origin were prospected. A magnetic susceptibility meter survey undertaken over the majority of Garden Field revealed that peaks of higher soil magnetisation were predominant in the eastern half of the existing enclosure, these higher readings may derive from settlement type activity. Lower readings were recorded in the western half of the field where potential colluvial deposits located on the side of the slope may be masking deeper lying areas of cultural enhancement. Information from OASIS Online Form.
